headings.title: Introduction and Principles of Special Bed Making
headings.content:
Special bed making involves arranging hospital beds in specific ways to meet distinct therapeutic, diagnostic, or clinical needs of patients. Unlike standard daily bed making, these techniques accommodate mobility limitations, surgical recovery, or acute respiratory distress. 

- **Cleanliness**: Maintain a high standard of hygiene to prevent nosocomial infections.
- **Smoothness**: Ensure the bottom sheet and draw sheet are free of wrinkles to prevent pressure ulcers.
- **Tucking**: Secure all linens tightly beneath the mattress to maintain structural integrity during patient movement.
- **Body Mechanics**: Keep the bed at a comfortable working height and maintain a wide base of support to protect your spine.
- **Infection Control**: Never shake used linen in the air; fold it inward and place it directly into the laundry hamper.

headings.title: General Equipment and Infection Control in Bed Making
headings.content:
Assembling the correct equipment before starting saves time and limits patient disturbance. The standard linen trolley carries items in the exact reverse order of use so the topmost item is placed on the bed first.

| Item | Purpose |
| --- | --- |
| Mattress pad | Protects the mattress from moisture and wear |
| Bottom sheet | Forms the clean foundation base |
| Draw sheet | Aids in repositioning and protects the middle section |
| Waterproof sheet | Blocks fluids from reaching the mattress core |
| Top sheet | Covers the patient and provides warmth |
| Blanket | Adds thermal insulation |
| Pillowcase | Covers the pillow cleanly |

Standard precautions require hand hygiene before and after the procedure. Always wear a plastic apron if the patient has draining wounds or profuse body fluids to protect your uniform from cross-contamination.

headings.title: Admission Bed
headings.content:
An admission bed, also called an unoccupied open bed, is prepared specifically to receive a new patient from the admission desk, emergency department, or outpatient clinic. The main goal is to welcome the patient with a clean, comfortable, and inviting unit while keeping the bed easy to get into.

The top covers—including the top sheet, blanket, and bedspread—are folded back in a specific triangle or fanfold pattern toward the side furthest from the entrance or towards the foot of the bed. This design minimizes handling when the client arrives, allowing them to transfer straight from a wheelchair or stretcher with minimal exertion.

headings.title: Operation Bed
headings.content:
An operation bed, or post-operative recovery bed, is designed to receive a patient returning from surgery. It must facilitate quick, safe transfer from a trolley and provide immediate access for monitoring vital signs and managing intravenous lines or drainage tubes.

- **Top Linens**: Fold the top sheet, blanket, and spread lengthwise to one side, or roll them tightly to the opposite side of the bed.
- **Protection**: Place a rubber draw sheet covered with a cotton draw sheet at the head or middle section where surgical drainage might occur.
- **Accessories**: Keep an emesis basin, tissue paper, suction tubing, and an oxygen mask close at hand on the bedside locker.
- **Warmth**: Place warm water bottles or a thermal blanket on the bed to combat postoperative hypothermia, ensuring skin protection barriers are in place.

headings.title: Cardiac Bed
headings.content:
The cardiac bed is arranged for patients experiencing severe heart failure, pulmonary edema, or acute respiratory distress who cannot lie flat. Lying down increases venous return to the heart, which overwhelms a failing myocardium and floods the lungs with fluid.

This bed uses an upright or semi-sitting posture known as the Fowler's or orthopneic position. Arrange multiple pillows behind the patient's back and head, and place a cardiac table or padded bedside tray across their lap. This allows the patient to lean forward, fixing their shoulder girdle so auxiliary respiratory muscles can assist with breathing. Soft pillows are also placed under the forearms to reduce muscle fatigue.

headings.title: Patient Safety, Comfort, and Ergonomics
headings.content:
Bed making requires attention to both patient comfort and nurse safety. Repetitive bending over low mattresses places severe strain on the lumbar spine. Always adjust the adjustable hospital bed to a comfortable waist height while changing linens, and return it to the lowest position before leaving the room to prevent fall injuries.

Side rails must be managed carefully. Lower the rail on your working side while keeping the opposite rail raised to prevent falls. Once bed making is finished, ensure all side rails are securely locked in place if ordered, call bells are within the patient's reach, and wheels are locked to prevent unexpected rolling during transfers.
